title: Naaman Washed in the Jordan; Gehazi's Greed
summary: Naaman, the commander of Aram's army, has a skin disease. An Israelite slave girl in his household points him to the prophet in Samaria, and after an angry refusal he washes seven times in the Jordan as Elisha says and is healed. He confesses that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel and offers gifts, which Elisha refuses; Elisha's servant Gehazi secretly takes some, and Naaman's disease comes upon him.
story: The Elisha stories move from the prophet's own circle to Israel's enemy. Aram (the kingdom of Damascus) is at war with Israel throughout these chapters, and its raiders have carried off an Israelite girl as a slave. Yet the LORD, the narrator says in the very first verse, had given Aram its victories through Naaman. The chapter continues the question Elijah asked Ahaziah in chapter 1, whether there is a God in Israel, and answers it from an unexpected direction: a pagan general comes to the knowledge of the LORD while Israel's own king cannot imagine that God might act. Gehazi, who has served faithfully so far, appears here for the last time at Elisha's side in his ministry, and his fall is the dark counterpart to Naaman's rise.
historical:
The chapter does not name the kings of Israel or Aram. The king of Israel is probably Jehoram son of Ahab (about 852 to 841 BC), and the king of Aram probably the Ben-hadad of chapter 6, though some date the story later. Aram and Israel fought for control of Gilead and the northern borderlands through most of the ninth century BC, with long periods of skirmishing and raiding between larger campaigns, which explains how bands of Arameans could carry off an Israelite girl.

Damascus sat in a fertile oasis watered by rivers flowing from the Anti-Lebanon mountains. The Abanah (or Amana) is usually identified with the Barada, which runs through Damascus, and the Pharpar with a river to its south. The Jordan, by comparison, is muddy and unimpressive for much of its length, which makes Naaman's complaint understandable. Naaman's gift was enormous. A talent was a weight of roughly thirty kilograms, so ten talents of silver alone was a king's ransom, along with six thousand shekels of gold and ten sets of fine clothing.
cultural:
The Hebrew word translated leprosy, tsara'at, covered a range of skin diseases and even mold on fabric and walls (Leviticus 13-14), and it probably did not usually mean what is now called Hansen's disease. In Israel it made a person ritually unclean and excluded him from the community. In Aram it seems not to have barred Naaman from command. Naaman's expectations were shaped by how healers worked in his world: he expected the prophet to come out, call on his god, and wave his hand over the diseased spot. Elisha's refusal even to meet him in person, and the command to wash in a foreign river, struck him as an insult.

In the ancient world gods were commonly associated with particular lands. Naaman's request for two mule-loads of Israelite soil (verse 17) reflects that belief: he wanted to worship the LORD on the LORD's own ground back in Damascus. Rimmon was the Aramean storm god, better known as Hadad; Rimmon (Akkadian Ramman, thunderer) was one of his titles, and the name appears in Zechariah 12:11 in the compound Hadad-rimmon. Naaman's duty to support his king's arm when the king bowed in the temple of Rimmon was a court ceremony he could not easily escape.
literary: The story is a study in reversals of greatness and smallness. It opens by stacking up Naaman's titles (commander, great man, highly regarded, mighty man of valor) and then adds a single Hebrew word, leper. The one who knows the way to healing is a small girl, a captive, and the people who talk Naaman into obeying are his servants. The great man must go down (verse 14) into the Jordan, and his flesh becomes like that of a little child, the same Hebrew word for small used of the slave girl in verse 2. Kings are shown as helpless: the king of Aram thinks a letter and money can buy a cure, and the king of Israel tears his clothes in panic. The final scene reverses the pattern once more. Naaman, the outsider, receives grace freely and becomes clean; Gehazi, the insider, grasps at payment and receives Naaman's disease. Elisha's question, “Is this the time to accept money and clothing” (verse 26), is the hinge of the ending.

outline.t: Naaman, the slave girl, and the letter to the king of Israel
Naaman washes seven times in the Jordan and is healed
Naaman's confession and Elisha's refusal of payment

doctrines.note: Naaman's healing is given, not bought. Elisha refuses every payment, and the cure comes through simple obedience to a word that seemed beneath him. The story became a classic picture of grace received by humility.

The LORD is God of the nations, not only of Israel. He gives Aram its victories, heals Aram's general, and draws him to confess that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel (verse 15). The first witness is an Israelite slave girl.

Naaman vows to sacrifice to no other god but the LORD, yet asks pardon for the ceremonial bow in Rimmon's temple. Gehazi, meanwhile, shows that greed can be its own idolatry, even in the prophet's own house.

words.note: Tsara'at, the disease translated leprosy. The term covered various serious skin conditions and made a person unclean under Israel's law. Its movement in this chapter is the story's frame: it leaves Naaman in verse 14 and clings to Gehazi and his descendants in verse 27.

Taher, to be clean or pure. It is the language of ritual purity from Leviticus, not only of physical cure. Elisha promises that Naaman will be clean, and Naaman's servants urge him, “Wash and be cleansed” (verse 13). His restoration is both healing and a kind of cleansing that brings him near to Israel's God.

Adamah, ground or soil. Naaman asks for two mule-loads of the adamah of Israel so that he can worship the LORD on it in Damascus. The request is theologically imperfect, since the LORD is not bound to a territory, but it is a real attempt to belong to him.

Teshu'ah, deliverance, salvation, or victory, from the same root as the names Joshua and Jesus. The narrator says that through Naaman the LORD had given teshu'ah to Aram (verse 1), a startling claim that Israel's God directs even the victories of Israel's enemies.

christ: Jesus himself preached from this chapter in the synagogue at Nazareth. He pointed out that there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time, yet none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian (Luke 4:27). His hearers were so enraged by the suggestion that God's mercy had passed over Israel for an outsider that they tried to throw him off a cliff. The story thus anticipates the gospel going to the Gentiles, a theme that runs through Luke and Acts. Jesus also healed lepers, touching them and declaring them clean (Mark 1:40-42), and in one scene only one of ten healed lepers, a Samaritan, came back to give thanks (Luke 17:11-19), much as Naaman returned to the man of God. Many Christians have seen in Naaman's washing a picture of baptism and of grace received without payment; this is a traditional application rather than something the Old Testament text claims.

hard.q: Why did Elisha tell Naaman to go in peace when he asked permission to bow in the temple of Rimmon?
hard.a: Naaman asks the LORD's pardon in advance for bowing in Rimmon's temple while his master leans on his arm, and Elisha answers only, “Go in peace” (verse 19). Readers have taken this in different ways. Many interpreters see pastoral wisdom: Naaman has just confessed the LORD alone, vowed to sacrifice to no other god, and asks forgiveness because his conscience is troubled. His bow is a court duty, not worship, and Elisha does not load a new believer in a pagan court with rules he cannot yet carry. On this reading the story shows God's patience with a young faith in a hard place. Other interpreters stress that go in peace is a customary farewell, not an approval of the act, and that Elisha simply leaves the matter between Naaman and God. Still others note the tension with the first commandment and with stories like Daniel's friends, who refused to bow at all (Daniel 3). The text does not resolve it. What it makes clear is that Naaman's heart has turned to the LORD and that he knows compromise needs forgiveness.

questions: Naaman nearly missed his healing because the cure seemed too simple and too humbling. What keeps proud people, including us, from receiving what God freely offers?
A captive slave girl, with every reason for bitterness, pointed her master to the prophet. How might God use you in a place you never chose to be?
Gehazi thought Naaman had been let off too easily and wanted payment. Where are you tempted to resent grace shown to someone else, or to profit from what God gives freely?
